questions.question: What is a cache stampede (thundering herd)?

options.text: Many requests simultaneously hitting the backend when a popular cache entry expires

questions.explanation: When a popular cache entry expires, many concurrent requests find it missing and all hit the database simultaneously. This can overwhelm the backend, causing cascading failures.

questions.question: A product page is cached with 5-minute TTL. At expiration, 1000 users are viewing it. What happens without stampede protection?

options.text: All 1000 requests hit the database simultaneously

questions.explanation: Without protection, all 1000 requests see cache miss and query the database. This sudden load spike can overwhelm the database, slow all requests, and potentially cause timeouts or crashes.

questions.question: How does locking prevent cache stampede?

options.text: Only one request fetches from backend; others wait for cache to be populated

questions.explanation: With locking: first request acquires lock and fetches data. Other requests wait (or return stale data). Once cache is populated, lock releases and waiting requests get cached data. Only one backend hit.

questions.question: What is 'probabilistic early expiration' for stampede prevention?

options.text: Some requests refresh cache before TTL expires, spreading the load

questions.explanation: As TTL approaches, requests have increasing probability of refreshing cache early. This spreads refreshes over time instead of all at once. XFetch algorithm implements this mathematically.

questions.question: What is 'stale-while-revalidate' and how does it help with stampede?

options.text: Serving stale cached data while one request refreshes in background

questions.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate: when cache expires, serve stale data immediately while triggering background refresh. Users get fast (stale) responses; only one background request hits backend. No stampede.

questions.question: Which techniques prevent cache stampede? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Locking ensures single fetch. Background refresh prevents expiration. Request coalescing groups concurrent requests into one backend call. Shorter TTL actually increases stampede frequency.

questions.question: What is request coalescing (request collapsing)?

options.text: Multiple identical concurrent requests share a single backend call

questions.explanation: Request coalescing: when multiple requests for the same key arrive simultaneously, only one fetches from backend. Others wait and receive the same result. Nginx, Varnish, and some caches support this.

questions.question: True or False: Cache stampede only affects read operations.
questions.explanation: Cache stampede is a read phenomenon—many reads hitting backend when cache misses. Write operations don't typically cause stampede (though they can cause other issues like write amplification).

questions.question: A cache warming job runs before a flash sale. How does this prevent stampede?

options.text: It distributes load across multiple cache nodes
Popular items are pre-cached, so they won't expire during peak traffic
It extends TTL values automatically during high traffic

questions.explanation: Cache warming pre-populates cache with expected hot data. If TTL is set appropriately, entries won't expire during the sale. No expiration = no stampede. Combine with longer TTL for sale duration.

questions.question: What is the 'dog-pile effect'?
questions.explanation: Dog-pile effect is another term for cache stampede—many processes 'piling on' the backend when cache expires. The terms are used interchangeably in caching literature.

questions.question: How can TTL jittering help prevent stampede?

options.text: Adding random variation to TTL spreads expirations over time

questions.explanation: Instead of all entries expiring at exactly 5 minutes, add random jitter (4.5-5.5 minutes). Expirations spread out, preventing synchronized expiration of related entries that could cause stampede.

questions.question: A system uses Redis for caching. Which Redis feature helps prevent stampede?
questions.explanation: SETNX (SET if Not eXists) can implement distributed locks. On cache miss, try SETNX lock_key. If successful, fetch and cache. If failed, another process is fetching—wait or return stale data.
